questions.q: Per this lesson, why shouldn't an architect design a solution straight from a stakeholder's literal first request?
options: Stakeholders are never worth listening to
The stated request is often a symptom of an underlying need, and building to the literal words risks solving the wrong problem
Literal requests are always technically impossible to build
Only developers, never architects, are allowed to talk to stakeholders
questions.explain: A stated request like 'add a related list' is often a symptom of a deeper need; the architect's job is to ask enough questions to find the real underlying need before designing.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a non-functional requirement, as distinguished in this lesson?
options: A rep must be able to see open cases for the account they're viewing
The page must load in an acceptable time even for a rep with thousands of related cases
Sales reps need a new button on the Account page
The feature must ship before the next board meeting
questions.explain: A load-time or scale expectation is a non-functional requirement — a quality the system must have, not a specific feature. Seeing cases is functional, and the board-meeting deadline is a constraint.

questions.q: In this lesson's framework, what is a 'constraint' as distinct from a requirement?
options: A constraint is just another word for a functional requirement
A fixed boundary the solution must fit inside -- like budget, an existing vendor contract, or a fixed deadline -- rather than a description of what the system should do
A constraint only applies to Apex code, never to declarative solutions
Constraints are optional and can always be ignored by the architect
questions.explain: Constraints describe the box the design has to fit inside -- deadlines, budgets, existing contracts, standing policy -- rather than describing a capability the system itself must have.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that skipping requirements-intake questions doesn't actually save time?
options: It does save time, with no downside
It moves the cost of discovering a missing requirement from the cheap design phase to the far more expensive build or post-launch phase
Requirements intake has no effect on project timelines either way
Skipping intake questions is illegal under Salesforce's terms of service
questions.explain: A scalability or security requirement discovered after a custom object and its data model are already live is far more expensive to fix than the same requirement caught in a short intake conversation.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does requirements analysis need to produce a written artifact, not just a conversation?
options: Because a later design decision is only defensible if it can be traced back to the specific requirement that drove it
Written documentation is purely a formality with no later use
Only non-functional requirements need to be written down
Verbal requirements are legally binding, so writing is redundant
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly connects this to documenting design decisions (Lesson 22) -- a decision is only defensible if you can point back to the requirement, tagged and sourced, that justified it.
